games.explanation: Toronto is priced like the better team tonight, which is a strange read on a matchup where Boston is the better team by a wide margin on the Elo board and Gausman keeps handing righties loud contact. The Blue Jays' ace has quietly allowed a 48.7% hard-hit rate to right-handed bats this year, which is exactly the wrong pool of hitters to face when Abreu and Contreras are stacked at the top of the order. Ranger Suarez, meanwhile, has been the steadier arm in this fight by nearly every ERA estimator you'd trust. The market saw a Gausman start and stopped reading; -135 on the sharper roster and the sharper pitcher is the whole pitch.

The market is treating this like a coin flip because Seattle is at home and Gilbert has the shinier surface stats, but the actual pitching gap tilts the other way. deGrom is the more efficient version of what Gilbert does, and Texas has the left-handed bats (Pederson, Nimmo, Carter) to force Gilbert into the part of the zone where his barrel rate against righties balloons past nine percent. The sim spits out a one-run game either way, which is exactly the kind of margin where you want to be getting a plus-ish number on the better starter. At -110 on the sharper arm in a projected 4-and-change slugfest, the price is doing you a favor.

Jose Soriano is a strikeout-light righty who walks the ballpark and gets barreled up when hitters do decide to swing, which is a strange profile to see priced as a coin flip against a lineup with Rafael Devers in it. Devers is running a .391 xwOBA against right-handers and Soriano hands out free passes to nearly 11 percent of them, so the top of this order should see plenty of traffic and plenty of mistakes. Whisenhunt is the shakier arm on paper, but Anaheim's park suppresses runs and homers enough to keep his margin for error wider than the raw numbers suggest. Getting the better team at a price that implies nothing of the sort is the entire pitch, and -106 barely charges for it.

Sanchez is a very good pitcher who happens to have one specific vulnerability, and the Yankees are built to press exactly that button. The lefty's numbers against righties are a full tier worse than his overall line, and New York rolls out a righty-heavy top of the order stacked with the kind of hard contact (Rice and Goldschmidt in particular) that turns his hard-hit rate against RHB, north of 44%, into actual damage. Warren isn't the pitcher Sanchez is, but he doesn't need to be in a park that plays this friendly to a lineup that slugs. Getting plus-money on the better team in a coin-flip game is the whole ballgame, and +158 is a price the market shouldn't be offering.
